feedback.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-7t{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,t>0.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-7t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+20{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-7\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+20{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-7\lambda +20] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-7\lambda +20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16)-16+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -4 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =4\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =4\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{4+2\text{i}} & ={t}^{4}{e}^{\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ {t}^{4-2\text{i}} & ={t}^{4}{e}^{-\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{4+2\text{i}}+B{t}^{4-2\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(t)$ as follows:

$$
y(t)={t}^{4}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=2.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=0$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =2{c}_{2}{t}^{3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2{c}_{2} \\ 1 & ={c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={t}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).
$$
